theory.intro: A quadrilateral has a line of symmetry if it can be folded so the two halves match exactly. It has rotational symmetry if it looks the same when turned about its centre.
facts: A **square** has $4$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of **order $4$**.
A **rectangle** has $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of **order $2$**.
A **rhombus** has $2$ lines of symmetry (its diagonals) and order $2$.
A general **parallelogram** has **no** lines of symmetry but rotational symmetry of order $2$.
steps: For a line of symmetry, imagine folding along the dashed line — do the halves match?
For rotational symmetry, count how many turns in one full circle give the same picture.
Match the shape to its known symmetry properties.

foundation.solution_text:
A square folds onto itself along its vertical and horizontal midlines and along both diagonals.
It has $4$ lines of symmetry.

The vertical and horizontal midlines are fold lines, but the diagonals are not.
It has $2$ lines of symmetry.

Each diagonal divides the rhombus into matching halves.
It has $2$ lines of symmetry.

Only the vertical diagonal folds the left half onto the right half.
It has $1$ line of symmetry.

No vertical, horizontal or diagonal fold makes the two halves match.
It has $0$ lines of symmetry.

The rectangle matches its starting position after a $180^{\circ}$ turn and after a full turn.
Its rotational symmetry is order $2$.

development.solution_text:
The square matches after turns of $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$.
Its rotational symmetry is order $4$.

A $180^{\circ}$ turn maps every vertex onto the opposite vertex.
Its rotational symmetry is order $2$.

No turn less than a full turn maps the unequal top and bottom vertices onto matching positions.
Its rotational symmetry is order $1$.

No fold line matches the two halves, so there are $0$ lines of symmetry.
A $180^{\circ}$ turn does match the shape, so the rotational symmetry is order $2$.

Folding along $EF$ swaps the left and right halves, and folding along $GH$ swaps the top and bottom halves.
The diagonals do not fold a non-square rectangle onto itself.
$EF$ and $GH$ are the lines of symmetry.

development.question_text: A quadrilateral has $4$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $4$. Name the quadrilateral.
development.solution_text:
Among the quadrilaterals studied, only a square has both $4$ fold lines and four matching positions in a full turn.
The quadrilateral is a square.

mastery.question_text: A mystery quadrilateral has exactly $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $2$. Explain why this information does not identify one unique quadrilateral. Name the two possibilities and say what extra observation distinguishes them.
mastery.solution_text:
A non-square rectangle and a non-square rhombus both have $2$ lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order $2$.
For a rectangle, the lines join midpoints of opposite sides; for a rhombus, the lines are its diagonals.
The positions of the lines distinguish the two shapes.

mastery.question_text: A square is first turned $90^{\circ}$ about its centre and then, from its starting position, folded across one diagonal. Explain what happens in each movement and state the two symmetry facts demonstrated.
mastery.solution_text:
The $90^{\circ}$ turn maps the square onto itself, demonstrating rotational symmetry of order $4$.
The diagonal fold also makes the two halves match, demonstrating that a diagonal is a line of symmetry.

mastery.question_text: A square card is cut into a non-square rectangle. Describe how both types of symmetry change.
mastery.solution_text:
The number of lines of symmetry changes from $4$ to $2$.
The order of rotational symmetry changes from $4$ to $2$.
